newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa talks focus on budget, rising stocks.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa talks focus on budget, rising stocks.

text.p: Cocoa nations began talks in London on Wednesday around a working agenda that seemed to be overshadowed by wrangling over house-keeping procedures.

But the three-day meeting of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) in London aims to make strides in providing a more accurate monitor of rapidly-growing stocks that have weighed on world prices recently, delegates said.
"Since stocks are overhanging more and more...it's important to try and get some accurate details," said Tim Mordan, the UK delegate and chairman of the ICCO executive committee.
An expert working group on stocks will meet on Thursday to review the latest available data from individual countries and urge noncommittal members to supply more figures.
Producers agreed in September to cut world output by a total of 90,000 tonnes over three years starting in 1996/97 to realise a stocks/consumption ratio of 34 percent from around 50 now.

But sceptical traders said the planned cuts would degenerate into a farce in the wake of the record harvest gathered by top producer Ivory Coast in 1995/96, ironically in the first year of the production management plan.
ICCO consumer delegates said increasing stocks would put more pressure on producers to implement the cuts more seriously.

But the leading UK cocoa analyst PCR Ltd already projected this month a lower 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) stocks/consumption ratio of 39 percent, the lowest for 10 years, pegging the world stocks at 1.078 million tonnes from 1.4 million last season due to less favourable weather.
ICCO delegates briefly touched on the issue of sharing the revenue from buffer stock sales and setting up a special reserve fund, a decision which must be made by March.
Producers and consumers are divided on how to allocate a last tranche of some $330 million expected to pile up in ICCO coffers from buffer stock sales over nearly five years.
Two-thirds of the revenue from selling 250,000 tonnes of cocoa has been re-distributed to members, mainly producers, who had to pay a levy when buffer stocks were introduced in 1986.
The money was also was used in financing ICCO expenses.
The sticking point now is to find a way of allocating the last tranche while securing a steady flow of income for the organization to prevent it from curtailing activities.

Consumers want a fund of a maximum of three million stg raised from the buffer stock revenue. Producers however are backing the ICCO executive director Eduard Kouame who favours a larger fund of 5-6 million stg to generate more interest income. Germany will make a proposal to the ICCO this week to set-aside the $4 million projected surplus profit from buffer stock sales for the fund.
"It might be an elegant way out of the problem," said Mordan.

Tuesday's agenda also included talks on setting up an environment fund. The Dutch and the Japanese governments have agreed to put put up the initial cash to identify projects with a view to increase awareness among producers.
"The intention is once the ball gets rolling other members will also contribute," said Mordan.
